A database index works like the index at the back of a cookbook. To find recipes with potatoes, you can look up “potatoes” and jump to the listed pages instead of reading every recipe. Similarly, a database index helps locate matching rows without scanning the entire table.

For example, an index on a customer table's email column can help the database quickly find the customer with a particular email address.

That convenience has a cost. The index takes up storage, and the database must maintain it when relevant data is added, changed, or deleted. This adds work to writes, even as it can speed up reads. Not every query benefits, so indexes should support the searches you actually need.

Daily counts include each person once per day they visit. The weekly count includes each person only once for the whole week.

Someone who visits Monday and Tuesday adds one to each day's count but only one to the weekly count. That's why adding the daily numbers can give a higher total; it's expected behavior.

We should label the views “daily unique visitors” and “weekly unique visitors” to make the difference clear.

We don't yet know whether the reminder emails reduced missed appointments. The missed-appointment rate fell from 18% in August to 12% in September, when reminders began—a drop of 6 percentage points. But September also had a different mix of appointment types and a new cancellation policy.

With no randomized comparison, the data shows an association rather than a demonstrated causal effect. The next useful check is to compare the same appointment types across both months. If feasible, a test with randomized assignment to receive reminders would help isolate their effect.
